Don’t Worry, Be Happy — Bobby McFerrin recorded “Don’t Worry, Be Happy” using only vocal and other sounds he made, without instruments; it became a US number one.
Tom’s Diner — Suzanne Vega first released “Tom’s Diner” as an a cappella recording; DNA’s unauthorized remix turned it into a dance hit.
The Great Gig in the Sky — Clare Torry improvised the wordless lead vocal on Pink Floyd’s “The Great Gig in the Sky”, built around Richard Wright’s composition.

assertion: Hide and Seek — Imogen Heap’s “Hide and Seek” is constructed around her multitracked voice processed through a harmonizer.

assertion: Medúlla — Björk’s “Medúlla” is composed almost entirely of human vocals, including choir, throat singing and beatboxing.
Blue Monday — New Order’s “Blue Monday” combined sequencers, synthesizers and electronic percussion and became the best-selling 12-inch single.
Autobahn — Kraftwerk’s album “Autobahn”, centred on its motorway-themed title track, brought the group international commercial success.
Oxygène — Jean-Michel Jarre recorded “Oxygène” in a home studio using analogue synthesizers and other electronic instruments.
Endtroducing..... — DJ Shadow’s “Endtroducing.....” was constructed almost entirely from samples and is recognised as a landmark of instrumental hip-hop.
Selected Ambient Works 85–92 — Aphex Twin’s debut album “Selected Ambient Works 85–92” collects tracks recorded by Richard D. James over several earlier years.
The Four Seasons — Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons” consists of four violin concertos accompanied by sonnets that describe scenes and weather in each season.
The Planets — Holst’s suite “The Planets” gives seven planets astrological characters, from Mars to Neptune, and does not include Earth.
Pictures at an Exhibition — Mussorgsky composed “Pictures at an Exhibition” in response to an exhibition of Viktor Hartmann’s art; its “Promenade” links several movements.
The Moldau — Smetana’s second “Má vlast” tone poem is “Vltava”, also known by the German name “The Moldau”, after the river that runs through Prague.
Scheherazade — Rimsky-Korsakov’s “Scheherazade” draws on “One Thousand and One Nights”, with a recurring solo violin associated with its storyteller.
